articles.title: Zelenskyy can leverage Moscow ties from comedy days to make peace deal, says former key aide
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earned his first millions in Moscow and should leverage those ties to negotiate with Vladimir Putin, says ex-aide.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's former spokesperson urged him Sunday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin face-to-face in Moscow, arguing that his past business and political connections in the Russian capital from years back could help him negotiate a peace deal there. Iuliia Mendel, who served as Zelenskyy's spokesperson from 2019 to 2021, told Fox News Digital that the former comedian had also made his first millions in Russia and should perhaps leverage those ties to pursue lasting peace. "When Zelenskyy was an entertainer, he often performed in Moscow," Mendel said, adding that the Ukrainian president "knows a lot of people from Putin's elite." "He actually professionally grew in Moscow and earned his first millions in Moscow, and today he pretends that he has nothing in common with them," Mendel said. RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY "He needs to go to Moscow and needs to agree on compromises that are acceptable," she said, before adding that Zelenskyy "doesn't need to play his maximalist games and to play this noble actor." Mendel's criticism came as Ukraine, Russia and the United States prepared for another round of technical-level peace talks, potentially in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland, in November. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have helped lay the groundwork for renewed negotiations that officials hope could finally lead to direct talks between the two leaders. Before entering politics, Zelenskyy had built a successful entertainment career. Beginning in the late 1990s, he performed with the comedy troupe Kvartal 95, competed on the Russian-language comedy program KVN and later worked as an actor, writer and producer in television and movies. From the late 1990s, he performed on Russian stages and at private parties and appeared in movies shown across former Soviet republics, Mendel claimed. She said that after Russia annexed Crimea and launched its war in Donbas in early 2014, Zelenskyy traveled to Russia to work on the comedy film "Eight New Dates" which was released in Russian theaters in 2015. ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE According to a report by Business Insider, many of Zelenskyy's movies were also in Russian and were marketed to a Russian audience, David Dodson, an American movie editor who worked with Zelenskyy told the outlet. "He was a well-loved comic, actor and performer in Russia, but after [the 2013-14] Maidan [Revolution], everything changed," Dodson said. "People need to realize that Volodya’s movies were very big in Russia. Most of his market was in Russia. He’s always been a popular comedy star in Russia," Dobson also clarified to GQ when asked if he directed the former actor in "Eight First Dates" in Russia, released in 2012. In 2013, the movie received the Russian National Movie Awards as the Best Russian Comedy of the Year. In 2019, Zelenskyy also promised to relinquish ownership of a Cyprus-registered company operating a film studio in Russia after investigative journalists revealed that he and his business partners still owned three Russian companies, according to the Kyiv Post. Zelenskyy's entertainment career made him a household name in Ukraine and other former Soviet republics before he entered politics and won Ukraine's 2019 presidential election with roughly 73% of the runoff vote on promises to fight corruption and pursue peace in eastern Ukraine. Mendel argued that Zelenskyy's promise to bring peace at the time stands in stark contrast to the devastating war that has crippled the country and defined much of his presidency. TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE "Zelenskyy became the president with 73% record support," Mendel said. "Because he promised to bring peace to Ukraine." "And now he has been presiding for almost five years (over) the largest war in Europe since World War II. This shows a lot." "When his country is bleeding, he needs to make a peace deal for his people," she said before adding that the leader "needs to put the interests of his people first, just for Ukraine to exist as an independent state." Whether Zelenskyy should travel to Moscow has, in fact, become a flashpoint in efforts to arrange direct peace talks. In 2025, Putin offered to host Zelenskyy for talks in Moscow, but the Ukrainian president rejected the invitation as Russian forces continued attacking Ukraine. "He can come to Kyiv," Zelenskyy told ABC News at the time, saying he could not visit Moscow while Ukraine remained under Russian missile attacks. In September, on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, Russian journalists pressed Zelenskyy on when he would visit Moscow. He replied, "On a missile." ZELENSKYY CONGRATULATES TRUMP ON TURNING 80 IN BIRTHDAY CALL, VOWS MORE UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AT G7 ON TUESDAY Mendel, however, argued that personal animosity between the two leaders has become the main obstacle to diplomacy. "Today there are diplomatic efforts to try to stop this brutal and bloody war that Russia started," she said. "But what we see now is a personal opposition between Zelenskyy and Putin that continues to grow into constant escalation in which people suffer tremendously, Ukraine's infrastructure, energy grid, and businesses are in ruins, and refugees are fleeing." Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. More than four years later, peace negotiations are deadlocked over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a lasting ceasefire. Moscow has demanded territorial concessions from Ukraine, including areas Russian forces do not fully control. Kyiv has rejected ceding sovereign territory and insists that any agreement include enforceable security guarantees against another Russian attack. RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN Mendel went on to praise President Donald Trump's efforts to break the diplomatic deadlock, calling him the first Western leader to "challenge the status quo" and consistently push for an end to the war. "For this reason, many Ukrainians place great hope in his ability to bring peace," she said. "A sustainable peace deal cannot be reached solely between Zelensky and Putin; it requires the involvement and initiative of a strong third party to halt the ongoing devastation." On Friday, the White House announced that first lady Melania Trump had helped broker a temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries, demining operations and civilian evacuations. An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in the devastated front-line town, many of them facing severe shortages of food, medicine and other essentials. The White House said the ceasefire would begin Oct. 29, although Ukrainian and Russian officials have indicated that operations could begin Oct. 27. Pope Leo also reportedly spoke with Zelenskyy and Putin about the humanitarian crisis, according to Vatican News. ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE "Melania Trump has become synonymous with the words of a saver and a hero, since she has brokered the deal for Oleshky," Mendel said. "This is something that is going to save around 2,000 people and that neither Ukraine nor Russia could have solved for months and months." "That is why, you know, what Melania Trump has done is actually a case to show that where two men are fighting, a woman can actually save lives," she added. "And this is the new approach that would show that peace really should focus on human lives, not on maps and territories." Mendel also criticized the influence of Zelenskyy's longtime ally Andriy Yermak on his diplomatic approach, arguing that the Ukrainian president has favored confrontation over compromise. "Mr. Yermak was teaching Zelenskiy to be a strong man in diplomacy. And what today we see is actually diplomacy that doesn't exist," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's a diplomacy of humiliation, diplomacy of constant threats, diplomacy of demands," Mendel added.

articles.title: Raids on NE drug cartels reveal illicit deals worth Rs 270cr
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a major crackdown on cross-border narco-hawala networks in northeastern states, multi-agency search operations by at least 38 teams at 38
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a major crackdown on cross-border narco-hawala networks in northeastern states, multi-agency search operations by at least 38 teams at 38 locations simultaneously, revealed illicit transactions of over Rs 270 crore, and led to arrest of six people and freezing of over 1,425 mule bank accounts. Properties worth over Rs 26 crore were also frozen or attached during the searches.“Modi govt’s lethal blow against drugs continues... Our agencies launched a barrage of simultaneous crackdowns across 38 locations in Assam, Mizoram and Manipur on Oct 23, smashing an international narco-cartel,” Union home minister Amit Shah said Sunday. Shah said India will hammer until the last nail is driven into the coffin of drug cartels.He also outlined govt’s policy of ‘zero tolerance’ against drugs and the strategic shift from a seizure-centric to a network-centric approach. The drive is part of Centre’s mission to eradicate drug smuggling syndicates by 2029.The latest searches were conducted on several premises in Aizawl, Champhai and Lawngtlai and Churachandpur and were related to cross-border trafficking of heroin, brown sugar and methamphetamine tablets from Myanmar and hawala settlement of drug proceeds. The operation was conducted by ED in coordination with NCB and Mizoram Police.ED has identified layered transactions of over Rs 270 crore, handled by illicit money exchangers, or hawala network, in Champhai, including Rs 125 crore in cash received from Assam, Nagaland, Bengal, Tripura and Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Panchang Today, October 26, 2026: Shukla Paksh 15 (Purnima), Ashwini, Shubh Muhurat, Rahu Kaal and More
articles.summary: Panchang Today is your everyday compass, built on the Hindu calendar’s deep sense of time and rhythm.
articles.body: Panchang Today is your everyday compass, built on the Hindu calendar’s deep sense of time and rhythm. It tells you what the Moon is doing, which star is active, and which parts of the day support work, worship, travel, and family choices. In a busy life, this small pause for Panchang keeps you connected to your cultural roots, and it also helps you act with more care, not just speed. Think of it like checking the sky before you step out, you plan better. Below are the important Panchang details for October 26, 2026 for India:Date & Day DetailsDate & Day DetailsOctober 26, 2026 falls on a Monday, a day that naturally leans toward steadiness, responsibilities, and the mind’s quieter routines. The Tithi is Shukla Paksh 15 (Purnima), and it ends at 09:41:18, after which the next Tithi begins, Krishan Paksh 1 (Pratipada(Ekam)). Purnima is the full Moon, the peak of the waxing fortnight. Spiritually, it’s like the Moon holds a mirror up to your emotions. Things become clear. Feelings rise, memories surface, and intentions made earlier in the month demand a practical step now.Because the Purnima Tithi completes at 09:41:18, the morning carries that full, luminous energy. This is supportive for prayer, gratitude, completing pending tasks, and family discussions that need warmth and honesty. After the shift to Pratipada(Ekam), the day’s tone subtly changes. Pratipada is the first step of the waning cycle, a clean page. It’s good for beginning simple habits, setting a fresh routine, and deciding what to reduce, clutter, overspending, gossip, unhealthy food, the usual suspects.The Nakshatra is Ashwini, ending at 17:41:15, after which Bharani takes over. Ashwini is ruled by the Ashwini Kumars, the divine healers and swift riders of the sky. That makes the day feel quick. You may want to rush, reply fast, finish fast, move fast. Use it well. Ashwini supports healing actions, starting exercise, visiting for checkups, learning a new skill, and timely travel. It also favours solutions that are simple and immediate, not overthought.By evening, Bharani begins. Bharani is linked with Yama, the keeper of dharma and discipline. So the day moves from speed to seriousness, like the breeze becoming firmer after sunset. If you’ve been avoiding a duty, Bharani’s influence can bring it right in front of you. Good. Handle it.The Moon sign is Aries 6.20, and it stays in Aries through the day, with a transition to Taurus at 27/10/2026 21:06:41. Aries Moon makes emotions direct. People speak plainly. Patience can run thin, especially in queues, traffic, and family group chats. Yet it’s excellent for taking initiative and not waiting for someone else to do the job.The Yoga is Vajra, ending at 14:16:55, and then Siddhi begins. Vajra has a tough, thunderbolt-like quality. It can make you determined, sometimes stubborn. Use it for disciplined work, not arguments. Siddhi later brings smoother outcomes, the kind where effort starts showing results. Karan also shapes the day’s flavour. Bava Karan lasts until 09:41:18, then Balava continues until 20:24:06. These are steady, workable Karans, helpful for routine progress, paperwork, household organisation, and commitments you can actually keep.Auspicious Timings (Shubh Muhurat)Auspicious Timings (Shubh Muhurat)Some days feel like the door opens easily if you knock at the right moment. Today has several such windows, and they’re worth using for prayer, decisions, and important steps.Brahma Muhurta runs from 2026-10-26 04:20:38 to 2026-10-26 05:11:22. This is the quiet, pre-dawn pocket when the mind is clean and receptive. If you’ve been trying to restart meditation, study, or a spiritual vow, this is the best time to sit with it. Even 15 minutes of japa or silent breathing here can change your mood for the whole day.Pratah Sandhya is from 2026-10-26 04:46:00 to 2026-10-26 06:02:06. It’s ideal for Surya arghya, simple prayers, and setting an intention for the day. On Purnima, morning worship feels fuller, like the heart has more space.Amrit Kalam appears from 2026-10-26 10:59:35 to 2026-10-26 12:28:47. This is a sweet stretch for important calls, submitting forms, starting a key meeting, or doing Satyanarayan Puja with focus. If you need to ask for help or approval, do it in this window. People respond better.Abhijit Muhurta, from 2026-10-26 11:18:58 to 2026-10-26 12:04:14, is another strong slot for beginning something that needs success and clarity. It’s particularly useful for interviews, signing something small but meaningful, or making a firm commitment to a health routine.Vijay Muhurta runs from 2026-10-26 13:34:46 to 2026-10-26 14:20:02. It supports winning energy. Use it to push a stuck task forward, speak to your boss about a pending matter, or tackle that one piece of work you keep postponing.In the evening, Godhuli Muhurta is from 2026-10-26 17:21:33 to 2026-10-26 17:46:55, and Sayahana Sandhya lasts from 2026-10-26 17:21:33 to 2026-10-26 18:37:39. These are perfect for lighting a diya, doing aarti, and calming the house atmosphere. On Sharad Purnima, twilight worship feels especially comforting.Night holds Nishita Muhurta from 2026-10-26 23:16:41 to 2026-10-27 00:07:25, a powerful time for deep prayer, mantra, and quiet inner work.Choghadiya also gives practical help. Day auspicious periods include Amrit @ 06:01, Shubh @ 08:51, Laabh @ 14:31, and Amrit @ 15:56. Night auspicious periods include Laabh @ 22:06, Shubh @ 25:17, and Amrit @ 26:52. Pick these for errands that matter, payments you must make, or family discussions that need a softer tone.Inauspicious TimingsInauspicious TimingsEvery day has a few rough patches, like a sudden patch of stones on an otherwise smooth road. The Panchang doesn’t ask you to fear them, it asks you to be smart.Rahu Kaal today is 07:26 to 08:51. There is also a verified Rahu Kaal window listed as 2026-10-26 07:27:01 to 2026-10-26 08:51:57. In essence, this morning period is best kept free from new beginnings. Don’t start a new business pitch, don’t sign a contract, and don’t make a big financial decision here. Keep your wallet closed today during this slot. If you must work, do routine work only.What should you do in Rahu Kaal? Choose inner work over outer risk. Sit for a short meditation, chant the Rahu mantra “Om Raam Rahave Namaha”, or simply read a few lines of a spiritual text. If you’re commuting, keep your mind quiet and avoid needless arguments.Yamaganda is from 2026-10-26 10:16:53 to 2026-10-26 11:41:49. This time can bring impatience and small obstacles. Avoid launching something new. Delay a hard confrontation if you can. If a meeting can be moved, move it.Gulika Kaal, shown as gulkai_kaal, runs from 2026-10-26 13:06:45 to 2026-10-26 14:31:41. This period is best for routine tasks and follow-ups, not for taking a big leap. Keep discussions practical. Avoid impulsive purchases.Dur Muhurtam appears twice, from 2026-10-26 12:04:14 to 2026-10-26 12:49:14, and again from 2026-10-26 14:20:02 to 2026-10-26 15:05:02. These are not ideal for initiating important work, sending risky emails, or making promises you can’t keep. Use these blocks for admin work, cleaning up your inbox, or finishing small tasks.Varjyam is from 2026-10-27 02:30:39 to 2026-10-27 03:58:33. It’s a time to avoid important starts and avoid restless late-night decision making. Sleep is a better choice.There’s also Baana (Roga) from 2026-10-26 06:02:06 to 2026-10-26 21:04:06. Treat this as a reminder to respect the body. Don’t skip meals and then overeat later. Don’t ignore small signs of fatigue.Panchaka runs from 2026-10-26 06:02:06 to 2026-10-27 06:02:40. Traditionally, Panchaka asks for extra care in planning and execution. It doesn’t mean you stop life. It means you double-check. Lock doors properly, confirm tickets, re-read messages before sending.Aadal Yoga is from 2026-10-26 17:41:59 to 2026-10-27 06:02:40, beginning just after Ashwini ends and the evening mood shifts. It can stir restlessness or sudden changes in plans. Don’t pick fights at home at night. Keep dinner light and conversations kinder.Choghadiya inauspicious periods also matter. Day inauspicious slots include Kaal @ 07:26, Rog @ 10:16, and Udveg @ 11:41. Night inauspicious slots include Rog @ 18:56, Kaal @ 20:31, and Udveg @ 23:42. During these, do regular work, not high-stakes work.Rahu Kaal Timings Across IndiaRahu Kaal Timings Across IndiaRahu Kaal changes across India because it is calculated from local sunrise, and sunrise differs from place to place due to longitude. So even on the same date, one region’s Rahu Kaal won’t exactly match another’s. The table below shows Rahu Kaal for major Indian cities, so you can follow the timing closest to your location and plan your important starts accordingly.CityRahu KaalMumbai08:02 - 09:29Delhi (NCR)07:52 - 09:16Bengaluru07:39 - 09:07Hyderabad07:39 - 09:05Chennai07:28 - 08:56Ahmedabad08:06 - 09:32Pune07:58 - 09:24Kolkata07:03 - 08:28Jaipur07:56 - 09:21Kochi07:42 - 09:11Lucknow07:36 - 09:00Indore07:53 - 09:19Guwahati06:52 - 08:17Chandigarh07:55 - 09:19Surat08:04 - 09:30Visakhapatnam07:20 - 08:46Nagpur07:39 - 09:05Coimbatore07:40 - 09:09Varanasi07:26 - 08:51Bhubaneswar07:11 - 08:37Sunrise, Sunset, Moonrise & MoonsetSunrise, Sunset, Moonrise & MoonsetSunrise is at 06:01:57, and that first light has its own message on Purnima. Wake up with purpose. Even a simple act, washing the face, offering water, standing quietly near a window, becomes a small reset. The day’s sunlight runs until sunset at 17:21:32. Use the middle hours wisely, because Aries Moon can make you burn energy fast. Pace yourself. Eat on time. Keep water nearby.Moonrise happens at 05:12:44 PM, and moonset is at 07:08:22 AM, Oct 27. articles.summary: A Beverly Hills home once owned by Hollywood actor Tom Cruise has changed hands for about $47 million, nearly a decade after the star sold it to
articles.body: A Beverly Hills home once owned by Hollywood actor Tom Cruise has changed hands for about $47 million, nearly a decade after the star sold it to billionaire Leon Black for $38 million in 2016. The property, which dates back to the 1930s, sits on approximately 1.2 acres and includes a main residence spanning around 10,000 square feet. Its latest sale marks another chapter in the history of the estate, which has remained largely out of public view.Tom Cruise’s former Beverly Hills home sold for $47 millionAccording to The Wall Street Journal, Black, the former chief executive of Apollo Global Management, sold the property for approximately $47 million. The buyer’s identity was not immediately known, and the house was not publicly advertised when the deal took place.The sale was handled privately, with local estate agents telling that the property had been quietly offered to potential buyers away from the open market. Linda May of Carolwood Estates and Fred Bernstein of Westside Estate Agency represented Black in the transaction, while the buyer was represented by real estate agent Kurt Rappaport.The latest transaction comes after a decade of ownership by Black and his wife, Debra Black, who purchased the estate through a limited liability company in 2016.What made the property notable during Cruise’s ownershipAs reported by the Los Angeles Times in June 2016, Cruise sold the Beverly Hills estate for $38 million after purchasing it in 2007 for $30.5 million. The actor had acquired the property from real estate developer and agent Kurt Rappaport, completing the purchase through a private transaction.The estate had been quietly offered for sale the previous year, with an asking price of $50 million. Its eventual sale price was therefore below that initial figure.Cruise's decision to sell the property was part of a broader effort to reduce his real estate holdings. The actor had also sold a gated compound in Hollywood Hills West for $11.4 million in 2015. His large retreat in Telluride, Colorado, had also been put on the market around that time. The Beverly Hills property was among the more significant assets associated with the actor's residential portfolio.Inside the 1930s estate and its groundsThe Los Angeles Times reported a gated and landscaped estate centred on a main house measuring more than 10,000 square feet. The residence contained 7 bedrooms, 9 full bathrooms and 35 rooms in total.The grounds offered several amenities, including a swimming pool, a tennis and basketball court, lawns and formal landscaping. Two detached structures also formed part of the estate, while a large motor court provided space for vehicles near the entrance.Why did Leon Black decide to sell the houseBlack and his wife sold the property because they no longer needed it, according to the WSJ. Their two adult children had lived and worked in Los Angeles for a period, but both subsequently returned to New York. As a result, the family had little reason to continue maintaining a large residence in Beverly Hills.Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management in 1990, stepped down as the firm's chief executive in 2021.The sale comes during a challenging period for Los Angeles propertyThe $47 million transaction stands out against a slower period for the Los Angeles residential property market. Local agents had attributed the slowdown over the preceding year partly to the devastating Los Angeles wildfires and the departure of wealthy residents for states with lower taxes.Against this backdrop, the sale of Black's Beverly Hills estate ranks among the area's larger property transactions in recent months. The estate has passed through two prominent owners over nearly two decades.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Data centre debate heats up ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
articles.summary: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
articles.body:
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map , a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000 operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.

This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom .

Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.

However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.

All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.

For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution . Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages , some experts say.

Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.

This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows , while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices .

With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.

Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections .

Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico , France, Indonesia and the UK .

But supporters say data centres are critical to national security , and the development of AI.

They also say they are good for the economy , attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.

A recent report by the Brookings Center suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.

The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.

But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.

As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.

This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.

But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.

One idea is to put data centres in space or on the Moon , where they could harness abundant solar energy.

Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones , reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.

articles.title: From India’s Gir forest to Edinburgh: New hope for big cats, as zoo welcomes two endangered Asiatic lion cubs for the first time in seven years
articles.summary: Imagine waiting for nearly a decade for something, and finally landing two of them!
articles.body: Imagine waiting for nearly a decade for something, and finally landing two of them!After seven years of waiting, Edinburgh Zoo finally has something exciting to celebrate: two brand new Asiatic lion cubs. These little arrivals aren’t just adorable; they have a much bigger meaning. Their birth on October 11, 2026, marks not only a rare event for the zoo but also highlights how vital conservation efforts are for one of the planet’s most endangered big cats. Their mother, Bindee, is a first-time parent, and their father, Jayendra, or Jay, as the keepers call him, seems to be taking everything in stride.What happened?Word got out about the cubs on October 22, when the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS), which runs Edinburgh Zoo, made the big announcement. Keepers had a front-row seat thanks to cameras in the lions’ den; they watched the births unfold and have been keeping a close eye on Bindee and her cubs ever since. At the moment, the zoo is keeping the family out of sight of visitors so that Bindee can bond with her new babies in peace. They've closed the lion habitat for now and promised to keep everyone updated about when things might reopen.It’s especially meaningful because the last time lion cubs were born at Edinburgh Zoo was in 2019, so there’s been quite a wait. The fresh arrivals aren’t just a win for the zoo; they’re a way to shine a spotlight on the real challenges facing Asiatic lions. In the wild, these cats hang on in just one small patch of India.As reported by the Edinburgh News, RZSS’s animal team leader, Alison MacLean, sounded genuinely delighted when talking about Bindee’s excellent care of her cubs. As for Jay, he’s apparently as laid-back as ever. But right now, the zoo’s staff care most about the health of the cubs, and the first few months are crucial. The family will stay mostly tucked away, with Bindee doing the heavy lifting as a new mom, and keepers watching quietly from behind the scenes.Meet Bindee and Jay: The lion parents with a storyWho are the proud parents, you ask? Bindee, ten years old, came to Edinburgh Zoo in 2024 from France, while Jay, fifteen, arrived in 2012 from Bristol Zoo, having been born in 2010. The keepers started guessing Bindee might be pregnant when they noticed her belly grow and her movements slow down. She became even more suspicious when she started changing up her den, pacing and prepping for her new arrivals.This birth is big news, especially since it’s Bindee’s first litter. Thanks to those cameras, zookeepers got to watch the birth unfold without interrupting Bindee’s natural instincts. The zoo says she’s doing well and bonding nicely with her cubs, much like any wild lioness would.Right now, the cubs are just getting used to life inside their den, and they’re not quite ready to meet the world. It’ll likely be several months before visitors get their first glimpse. As for their names? No update on that yet. The zoo is keeping everything under wraps, putting the little lions’ well-being above all else. The lion habitat stays closed while the animal-care team waits for just the right moment.Why the birth matters: The plight of Asiatic lionsNow, about the significance of these cubs, it goes way beyond Edinburgh. Asiatic lions, known scientifically as Panthera leo persica, have been nearly wiped out by hunting and the destruction of their habitat. In the past, they roamed across western and southern Asia. Today, their last wild survivors stick to a single region: the Gir forest and its surrounding areas in Gujarat, India.That’s exactly why there’s a glimmer of hope in this story.As shared by PIB (Press Information Bureau), in India’s 2025 count, officials recorded 891 lions, up from 674 just five years prior. That’s a 32% jump, and the numbers include cubs, subadults, and adults scattered across the lion landscape, even outside the main protected area. But a bigger population doesn’t mean the species is safe. When a species lives in just one area, it’s super vulnerable. Disease, disasters, and even accidents can threaten the whole group at once. Meanwhile, lions that wander outside the protected zone face dangers from roads, trains, and clashes with people and livestock.So, they’re still in trouble. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the Asiatic lion as endangered. Protecting their habitat, providing veterinary care, monitoring populations, and finding ways to reduce human-lion conflict — all of this is essential if these lions have a chance at a future.How Edinburgh Zoo fits into the bigger pictureEdinburgh Zoo doesn’t just display lions; it plays a real part in conservation. The RZSS runs the place and takes part in the European Endangered Species Programme for Asiatic lions. The programme tries to keep the population healthy and genetically diverse inside zoos, while boosting awareness, funding research, and supporting lions in the wild. So, these two new cubs are a lot more than just cute faces; they matter to the survival of the entire species, whether in zoos or back home in India.The birth also gives Edinburgh Zoo a chance to teach visitors about wildlife conservation, showing how the lives of animals in captivity really connect to the challenges their wild cousins face. Sure, breeding in zoos can’t replace wild populations, but it helps keep genetic diversity, fosters research, and grabs people’s attention, which is half the battle when it comes to saving endangered creatures.For now, Bindee and her cubs are hunkered down out of sight, slowly growing and getting stronger before their big debut. After so many years without lion cubs, the zoo’s staff are thrilled. It’s a feel-good moment, and a reminder that every new cub matters when a species is fighting for survival.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Todd Blanche challenges Dana Bash for only citing part of Constitution during heated election clash
articles.summary: Todd Blanche demanded CNN show the full Elections Clause in the Constitution on air after Dana Bash highlighted only the first portion during a tense legal debate.
articles.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche confronted CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday after the network highlighted only the first portion of the Constitution's Elections Clause during a heated exchange on "State of the Union" over the Justice Department's lawsuit concerning two candidates with similar names in Alaska's closely watched Senate race. Blanche pushed back as Bash referenced the Alaska Supreme Court's earlier ruling allowing Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who shares a name with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, to remain on the ballot. The attorney general demanded that CNN display the remainder of the constitutional provision, which grants Congress authority to make or alter regulations governing congressional elections. "Conveniently, you put up the Constitution on your screen, but you highlighted only the first clause. Why don't you show the next clause to your viewers, which says that Congress is allowed to pass laws to make sure that that happens? Put that back up there," Blanche said. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO The exchange centered on Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution, which gives state legislatures authority to establish procedures for congressional elections while permitting Congress to enact or modify those regulations. Blanche argued that the second half of the provision supports the federal government's intervention under existing federal statutes. "The second clause says that the Congress may at any time by law, and we have a law, and that's the law that we're relying on when we filed suit earlier this week," Blanche said. The Justice Department’s lawsuit relies on the National Voter Registration Act, arguing that allowing a candidate who, according to the DOJ, intends to confuse voters to remain on the ballot undermines election integrity. The complaint asks the court to delay election certification if votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could alter the final outcome. The DOJ's complaint accused the challenger of deliberately attempting to mislead voters by using a name similar to the incumbent's. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS Media Research Center President David Bozell criticized Bash's presentation of the constitutional language in a statement to Fox News Digital, accusing CNN of failing to provide viewers with the complete provision. "An anchor who hands viewers half a provision on election integrity is running a magic act, and the trick fell apart on live television. Bash's job is to give the audience the full text up front. CNN owes its dozens of viewers the whole clause, and a better editor," Bozell said. The DOJ lawsuit follows a June ruling by the Alaska Supreme Court allowing the challenger to appear on the ballot despite objections from state election officials. The court left the question of how his name should appear to the state's Division of Elections. "Daniel J. Sullivan decided to run for Senator in 2026 as a Republican with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him," the complaint states. BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD Republicans have accused the challenger, a retired teacher from Petersburg, of attempting to siphon votes from the incumbent. Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those accusations and maintained that his candidacy is legitimate. President Donald Trump also addressed the controversy Friday while speaking to reporters in Florida, acknowledging that he personally encouraged the Justice Department to pursue legal action. "I'm the one that said, do it," Trump said. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: More than 10 lakh vehicles in neighbouring NCR areas of Gurgaon, Faridabad, Noida, Greater Noida and Ghaziabad could be affected by Delhi's
articles.body: NEW DELHI: More than 10 lakh vehicles in neighbouring NCR areas of Gurgaon, Faridabad, Noida, Greater Noida and Ghaziabad could be affected by Delhi's decision to prohibit the entry of vehicles below BS6 emission standards from Nov 1, 2026 to Jan 31, 2027, according to transport department estimates.Gurgaon and Faridabad together have nearly 2 lakh vehicles that do not meet BS6 standards, of which around 70% are BS3 and BS4 vehicles.Around 50,000 commercial vehicles in the two Haryana districts are also below BS6 standards, according to an estimate by the transport department.Strict checks at border points to enforce curbsMore than 4 lakh vehicles fall below the BS6 emission standard in Noida and Greater Noida, with BS4 vehicles accounting for over half of the total. These are predominantly petrol cars. Ghaziabad has around 4 lakh vehicles that do not meet BS6 standards, a senior transport department official told TOI.The restriction on vehicles registered outside Delhi that fall below BS6 emission standards will remain in force from Nov 1, 2026, to Jan 31, 2027, as part of the city's winter pollution control plan. The move could affect vehicle owners who travel regularly from neighbouring NCR cities to Delhi.BS6 vehicles comply with the country's latest and most stringent emission standards for motor vehicles. The Bharat Stage norms prescribe legally enforceable limits on air pollutants emitted by internal combustion engines.To enforce the restriction, authorities are strengthening checks at Delhi's entry points. Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras are being used at border checkpoints and strategic lanes to automatically read vehicle registration plates, officials said.AI-powered cameras are intended to help identify vehicles entering the capital. Authorities are also fortifying entry points to physically stop non-BS6 vehicles from crossing into Delhi from neighbouring areas, including Noida, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad.Around 300 personnel from transport department enforcement teams will be deployed as part of the enforcement arrangements.The restrictions come as Delhi prepares for the winter pollution season, when the capital faces deteriorating air quality. The ban specifically covers vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS6 standards.India introduced its first formal vehicle emission framework, known as India 2000 and equivalent to Euro 1, in 2000. The country subsequently moved through BS2, BS3 and BS4 standards before transitioning to BS6. articles.title: US Marine indicted over alleged murder of woman in Okinawa
articles.summary: Japanese prosecutors have indicted a US Marine on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Okinawa earlier this month, multiple Japanese media outlets have reported, in a case that has prompted renewed outrage over the conduct of US troops in the country.
articles.body: Japanese prosecutors have indicted a US Marine on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Okinawa earlier this month, multiple Japanese media outlets have reported, in a case that has prompted renewed outrage over the conduct of US troops in the country. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old Marine assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force at Futenma Air Station, is charged with killing a woman by strangling her with a phone cord at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital, and stealing her backpack containing a wallet, public broadcaster NHK and others, reported on Sunday. Anna Yagi, 39, was found unresponsive in her hotel room and pronounced dead at the scene on the morning of October 3, Okinawa police previously told CNN, adding the cause of death was suffocation. Ballard was arrested less than 24 hours later while walking around the city, police said. CNN is working to determine Ballard’s legal representation. The prosecutors have not disclosed whether the suspect has admitted or denied the charges, according to NHK. Okinawa police previously told CNN Ballard denied the charges. The Naha District Public Prosecutors Office declined to comment on the case to CNN on Monday. A spokesperson for the III Marine Expeditionary Force told CNN the US military recognizes “the seriousness of the charges and will continue to cooperate fully with Japanese authorities in their ongoing investigation as the legal process moves forward.” Yagi’s family said in a statement they “hope the real culprit will face up to what he has done and make amends.” Yagi’s “life was cut short at the young age of 39,” they added. Arrest sparks protests, backlash The case against Ballard is the latest in a string of allegations against US personnel in Okinawa, which has been the site of longstanding anger and protests over the American presence on the island chain. Okinawa hosts several US military facilities and is home to about 30,000 US troops and their families. Ballard’s arrest sparked local protests and condemnation from politicians and leaders in Japan, including Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who said her government “strongly protested” to the US and called for “thorough discipline among US military personnel, and comprehensive measures to prevent the recurrence of crimes and accidents.” Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the alleged murder “leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military’s efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective.” Following Ballard’s arrest, US troops on the island were placed under a monthlong curfew and were required to undertake training on “standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community.” Last year, US Marine Lance Corporal Jamel Clayton, 22, was sentenced to seven years in prison after he was convicted of strangling and sexually assaulting a woman in Okinawa. In 2024, US Air Force member Brennon R. E. Washington, 25, was sentenced to five years for kidnapping and raping an underage girl. In 2016, tens of thousands of people demonstrated calling for an end to the US military presence on Okinawa following the killing of a local woman by a civilian worker stationed at the US Kadena Air Base. CNN’s Junko Ogura and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

articles.title: Anthropic taps a deep well of distrust as it eyes its Australian AI debut
articles.summary: The first rainfall in months splashes off the windshield as the local mayor drives to the site of what could be Anthropic’s first AI data center in Australia.
articles.body: The first rainfall in months splashes off the windshield as the mayor of Western Downs Andrew Smith drives to the site of a proposed AI data center behind a cattle feedlot in rural Queensland. It’s feeding time and 16,000 cattle are standing under shade sails waiting for a passing truck to shoot grain into their troughs. Agriculture is the biggest employer in this area, 260 kilometers (131 miles) west of Brisbane. But beneath the rich vertosol soils that sustain year-round crops lies a massive gas field that’s also turned the region into an energy hub. Now the AI data center industry has come knocking with a $22 billion proposal from Singaporean developer Zerra DC to build the Western Downs Digital Park, one of Australia’s largest AI data centers, with four buildings each the size of five football fields, and temporary accommodation for 1,500 workers during the construction phase. The project hasn’t been formally approved. But its first major tenant, US giant Anthropic, has already signed a lease, setting the stage for the company’s Australian debut. Smith says the enthusiastic state government has assured him that the decision will fall to the local council. It’s a hefty responsibility in a febrile environment where a growing number of Australians are expressing their opposition to AI, amid an unresolved national debate about the country’s place in the AI boom. American AI giants have turned on the charm, praising the nation’s open spaces, commitment to renewable energy, and trusted position as a partner in the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance. “We are working towards having significant capacity hosted in Australia,” David Masters, Anthropic’s head of policy for Australia and New Zealand told CNN. But the Australian government is treading carefully, leading calls for responsible growth “with guardrails” – for many reasons, including a recent breach of its healthcare data and warnings from within tech companies, including Anthropic, that AI advances are outpacing controls. Standing beside the proposed data center site in the Western Downs, Smith says he sees an opportunity to diversify the local economy, create jobs for future generations and give the region’s youth a reason to come home. Though he insists a decision hasn’t been made on the data center, the mayor added: “Our role is to look ahead, and if we want to maintain our communities 20 or 30 years ahead, we need to be progressive. And sometimes you do need to be brave.” AI centers run on fossil fuels Back in July, the Australian prime minister vowed to require tech companies to power AI data centers with renewable energy, among a raft of requirements. Within a month, he’d backed down. Queensland negotiated an exemption, so that if approved, the Western Downs Digital Park will be directly connected to the grid, running on a mix of energy sources that includes fossil fuels – coal and natural gas from one of Australia’s largest gas basins, which sits directly below the site. More than 6,000 unconventional gas wells pierce the land around this region, extracting gas that’s mostly sold to foreign markets. Accessing coal seam gas requires a process called “de-watering” – pumping out groundwater to relieve pressure and free the gas. And that lies at the heart of AI opposition in this community – this place is dry. Months without significant rain have browned the grass and trees. Rainwater tanks were running low until a downpour last week. Many farmers rely on bore water, but some say their wells have been pumped dry by the gas industry, and their water is now being offered to the developers to help build the AI data center. “That’s stolen water,” thundered grain farmer Bev Newton, who’s engaged in a long-running dispute with a gas company that she believes will end in court as she seeks payment to replace her bore water. Bev and Wayne Newton rely on heavy downpours – when they come – to fill the family’s water catchment. But they say some of their farmland is sinking, due to subsidence caused by the coal seam gas industry, making future flows difficult to predict. Rainwater will be harvested and recycled to sustain workers during operations, Zerra DC says, but Bev Newton points to a shared problem: “No amount of surface water catchment, be it shed roofs into tanks, works if you don’t have rain that falls from the sky.” Zerra DC says it’ll cool the data center using air-cooling technology, which requires far less water than the evaporative methods that have sparked protests from the US to India to Indonesia. But air-cooling technology is more energy-intensive, and residents already fear that the center’s energy demands could strain the network, raise electricity prices, encourage more gas extraction, more de-watering, and potentially more subsidence – adding more stress to their daily worries about water. Zerra DC says the project’s phased development will give it time to work with its customers – like Anthropic – to create new power sources, and while demand for power will increase, it says its battery conditioning system will buffer the grid from load spikes to help “stabilise power prices.” Anthropic says it intends to enter into virtual power purchase agreements – or deals struck with energy providers – to procure more power for the grid, with a preference for renewables. “The source for this generation will be new build projects – but precisely which projects is an ongoing discussion,” said Masters, from Anthropic. Rogue AI agents As Prime Minister Anthony Albanese prepared to deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in late September, a surprise gift arrived to back his case for tougher guardrails on AI. An agent from Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI had hacked the nation’s healthcare data. It accessed statistics but not personal information, making it a largely benign attack, but one that sent an ominous warning. After receiving a call from Albanese, OpenAI’s Sam Altman apologized and vowed to win back Australians’ trust. Less than two weeks later, at an Australian parliamentary committee hearing on AI, Anthropic’s international special envoy Jeff Bleich invited the country’s leaders to “step up to” the choice of AI. “If Australia takes this opportunity and gets the balance right, it will not simply participate in the AI era; it will shape it,” he said. Anthropic said the proposed center at Western Downs won’t be used to train large language models – because Australia’s tough copyright laws currently ban it – but it will answer questions to its Claude AI model. So, CNN asked Claude whether the data center application should be approved based on the publicly available information, a petition to the Queensland parliament against the proposal signed by more than 23,000 people, and local media reports – removing any bias that may have crept in due to Anthropic’s involvement in the project. Claude’s response: “Don’t decide before public notification and independent technical assessment of water, power, noise, and workforce. Hold the public meeting residents asked for. Be clear about who actually holds the decision if the state steps in.” AI proposal troubles town In a well-lit pub in Dalby, the closest major town to the proposed data center, cutlery clinks as elderly diners relax over a Friday-night meal. A few residents have agreed to meet in a private room to share their concerns, which range from water to power to the “dumbification of humanity.” “Just because big companies over in the US are advocating for AI usage doesn’t mean that we should follow,” said Corey Cora, who works in retail. “Most people in the community won’t even know about this until it’s too late,” added telecoms worker Joel Holtham. In the last few weeks, Zerra DC has held pop-up information sessions in the town, population 12,000, to answer residents’ questions. Before retiree Beris Furner dropped in for a chat, he supported the AI expansion. “I thought this is fantastic for Dalby. A great opportunity for future generations coming along for the kids, if they’re that way inclined, to train and work in a place like that,” said Furner. But after asking questions of Zerra staff, he now believes the council’s pushing ahead with a speculative proposition without enough community buy-in. “We need a public meeting. It’s such a massive deal for the town,” he said. Mayor Smith said the council wouldn’t be holding public meetings on the matter: “We always stay away from town hall meetings. It generally doesn’t end up well.” Asked if it was also up to the council to provide residents with an alternative source of information, Smith said: “We need to stay in our lane. We aren’t the experts on data centers. So, for us to be in the public talking about data centers would, I think, be wrong.” “We will stay out of the larger data center AI discussion.” Calls for a pause The lack of discussion is frustrating some residents who feel their home is being pulled into the competitive AI race between the US and China, exposing them to a future they don’t necessarily want. “It feels like we’re in a weird sci-fi movie and everything’s just spiraling out of control really quickly,” said Ahri Tallon, from the Darling Downs Environment Council. “We’re really calling on the government, as many people are around the world, to put a moratorium on AI and data centers and really take the time to work with the community to go through the deep ethical conversations that we need to think about in terms of how much can this technology be potentially for good, but how much could it be for bad?” Others look at the practicalities of sharing their home with a water- and power-hungry industry, and a future where there may be more jobs for their children to come home to, but perhaps another set of challenges that will ultimately drive them away. Shay Dougall took a job in workplace health and safety during the construction of a coal seam gas processing facility 20 years ago, married a farmer, and now works as a postdoctoral research associate with the University of Sydney examining the impact of industrialization in rural areas. She’s seen firsthand the distress of farmers who’ve strained under the expansion of the gas industry, then renewables, and she now fears the same is happening with data centers. “Those people not only are hosting this industrialization, but they’ve been impacted by the changes to the climate as a result of it. So, it’s just a double whammy,” she said. In Queensland, the government hasn’t ruled out the approval of new coal-fired power stations to support the expansion of AI in the state – if tech companies pay for them. The federal member of parliament for the area has praised the possibility of more coal production. “The proposed Western Downs data centre alone has a peak capacity of 2.16 gigawatts, more than a quarter of Queensland’s daily electricity consumption. You cannot run that on renewables alone. The coal is here…” he said in a Facebook post. The state government told CNN it’s developing a framework for the approval of data centers that “puts community support at the forefront of decision making.” As Anthropic prepares to launch an IPO – potentially valuing the company at $1.5 trillion – it’s promising to spend tens of millions of dollars in the areas it operates. To that end, it’s hiring a “community engagement manager” in Australia whose role will be to “make Anthropic a trusted, visible, and valued neighbour.” But the problem in Dalby is that trust dried up with the bore water, and some residents don’t see the same opportunity touted by AI companies, the council and the government – just more potential problems. Rather than being a drain on resources, Smith, the mayor, sees interest from the AI industry as one way to get the water flowing. He wants billions of dollars of investment for new water infrastructure in the region – and is looking at the state and federal governments, as well as developers – to get it. Smith said he’s having “almost daily” conversations with other data center developers about moving to the area, part of a national shift that’s seeing more development applications lodged for larger facilities, further away from metro regions, according to energy intelligence platform RenewMap. “We know that the one guarantee we have is that data centers are a part of our nation’s future,” said Smith. “The question here on the Western Downs is do we want them here?” “Do we want to take the opportunity that is there, or do we want to give that opportunity to somebody else?”

articles.title: How Lula beat Bolsonaro, broke records and halted the right-wing wave aligning Latin America with Trump in 20 days
articles.summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made history on Sunday, setting a record for Brazil and the rest of Latin America by becoming the first president to win a fourth term – and he did so days before turning 81, an age when many other leaders decide to leave politics behind.
articles.body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made history on Sunday, setting a record for Brazil and the rest of Latin America by becoming the first president to win a fourth term – and he did so days before turning 81, an age when many other leaders decide to leave politics behind. The Brazilian president’s remarkable comeback against his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, also set another record. Since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985, no president has managed to overturn a first-round defeat. The Workers’ Party candidate added more than 10 million votes in the three weeks between the two rounds of voting, while his rival gained just 3.6 million. The margin was decisive enough for Lula to secure a larger lead than he did in 2022, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father and the incumbent president at the time. The comeback also allows Lula to remain the leading figure of the regional left as the right advances in other countries across Latin America, many of whose governments are now aligned with Donald Trump’s White House. As his father did four years ago, Flávio Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result and announced that he would seek to have the election annulled through the courts. The senator challenged Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours, arguing that the uneven application of the measure had undermined equal voting conditions. “It is impossible to recognize the election results given the circumstances in which these events unfolded,” he said. Bolsonaro’s statement did not dampen celebrations over Lula’s historic achievement. But the right’s political strength could hinder the smooth functioning of his new administration. The victory confirms Lula’s political staying power. Yet Bolsonaro’s defeat does not weaken the right’s grip on Congress and state governments. That is the paradox of Lula’s next term: a historic electoral triumph and limited room to govern. What explains Lula’s unexpected victory? Geography helps explain how Lula overturned his first-round deficit. In Minas Gerais, the state with Brazil’s second-largest electorate, he went from losing by nearly 590,000 votes to winning by about 99,000 — a swing of roughly 690,000 votes in the margin between the two candidates. The state, which has backed the winner of every direct presidential election since 1989, once again voted in line with the national result. Although Flávio retained his lead in the states of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, Lula won their capitals, Brazil’s two largest cities, and reversed the first-round result in the city of Rio. His gains were reinforced by victories in all nine northeastern states and higher voter turnout. Abstention fell from 21.08% in the first round to approximately 19.2% in the runoff, bringing nearly three million more Brazilians to the polls. That additional participation cannot be attributed entirely to Lula, but it underscores the importance of mobilizing those who had not voted: in the first round, the gap between the candidates was just over 2.2 million votes. The battle was also fought on Brazilians’ phones. After finishing second in the first round, Lula stepped up his digital mobilization efforts to expand his reach and turn support into votes. The challenge was not simply to persuade undecided voters, but to get those who already preferred him to show up at the polls. The push was accompanied by last-minute measures and proposals aimed at voters’ concrete concerns. Lula signed into law a measure raising the revenue threshold for individual microentrepreneurs, proposed new initiatives to renegotiate consumer debt and advocated ending online betting, whose expansion has contributed to household indebtedness. On security, he even embraced a traditional right-wing position: he backed lowering the age of criminal responsibility for particularly serious offenses. The move was intended to respond to demands for a tougher approach to crime, another major issue in the election. The victory allows Lula to remain in power, but it also obliges him to meet the expectations he raised to secure it. More than one challenge ahead Lula’s first challenge after celebrating his victory will be legislative. Right-wing parties will hold 303 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies, compared with 124 for the left and 86 for the center. In the Senate, the right will control nearly two-thirds of the seats. That does not make every one of those lawmakers an automatic opponent, but it means Lula will have to build alliances beyond his own base both to advance his proposals and to defend his government’s priorities. The map of state governments also shows the strength the conservative camp retains. Across the two rounds of voting, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won five governorships, while the Republicans and the Progressive Party (PP) secured four each. The Workers’ Party (PT) won four. The Social Democratic Party (PSD), which brings together politicians with different political alliances, secured another five. Negotiations with those governors will be another challenge for Lula, who will need cooperation at the state level to implement his policies. “Once we win the election, we no longer have opponents. I have to govern for 215 million people,” Lula said in his victory speech. He also addressed the challenge of negotiating with a more conservative legislature: “I didn’t choose Congress. The people did. And that is the Congress with which I will vote, work and get things done.” The most immediate challenge will be to turn economic gains into relief that Brazilians can feel in their daily lives. Perceptions of the economy were among the main sources of erosion in Lula’s support during the campaign. Lower inflation does not bring prices back to their previous levels, and improvements in employment do not necessarily offset the burden of debt and household expenses. Dissatisfaction with the cost of living will remain after the election. Addressing that discontent will be harder because of fiscal constraints. Debt, the deficit and high interest rates limit the government’s ability to increase spending and foreshadow disputes over how to fund campaign promises without jeopardizing social programs. With an unfriendly Congress, decisions about who pays and where cuts are made will also test Lula’s ability to negotiate. Security will be another source of pressure. Lula will have to respond to demands for tougher measures against crime, as the right has made a hard-line approach one of its main political platforms. In the final stretch of the campaign, he signaled a tougher stance by expressing his willingness to lower the age of criminal responsibility to 16 for serious offenses, a measure championed by the right and backed by broad public support. It remains to be seen whether he will turn that campaign signal into a concrete proposal. He will also face the challenge of preparing a successor for a left whose ability to win presidential elections remains closely tied to his own political stature. Regional autonomy and isolation The challenges extend beyond Brazil’s borders. The progressive leader’s comeback prevented Trump from securing the crown jewel of a wave of victories by right-wing candidates aligned with the White House. As head of Latin America’s largest economy, with China as its top trading partner, Lula’s government has used Brazil’s economic weight to push back against Washington’s trade and political demands — a degree of autonomy few of its neighbors can attempt. A Bolsonaro victory, by contrast, would have marked a major shift in Washington’s efforts to secure its dominance in the hemisphere and curb Beijing’s reach. Yet Lula faces a highly challenging regional landscape and risks being largely isolated. “Lula faces a very different political environment from the one that existed when he first took office, during the pink tide. Back then, he had several regional allies and could play both sides to Brazil’s advantage,” Michael Paarlberg, an associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University and a researcher at the Center for International Policy (CIP), a Washington-based think tank, told CNN. The region’s political landscape is also different from the one Lula faced when he began his third term in 2023, when allies such as Alberto Fernández in Argentina, Gabriel Boric in Chile and Gustavo Petro in Colombia were in power. “Lula is unlikely to spend his political capital pushing regional integration initiatives such as Unasur (Union of South American Nations), as he did during his first terms. Lacking ideological allies, he will exercise that leadership through Brazil’s economic weight — its investments, trade and Mercosur,” Paarlberg added, referring to the South American trading bloc. Looking toward Trump and the US midterm elections As he prepares for his fourth term, Lula will have to decide how to approach relations with the United States. “Brazil does not belong in anyone’s backyard,” Lula said at the United Nations in September, in a message directed at Washington. Yet he has also acted cautiously. When the United States imposed a new round of tariffs on Brazilian goods in the middle of the year, he left open the possibility of retaliatory measures. “Lula has shown an ability to adapt to Trump. He has balanced occasional harsh criticism with conciliatory gestures,” the analyst said. “For Lula, sovereignty does not necessarily mean confrontation; in fact, he believes confrontation does not necessarily strengthen sovereignty. (…) Lula is not ideologically anti-American, nor does he have difficulty working with right-wing governments,” he added. Paarlberg also said the reelected president would closely follow the US midterm elections, in which “his position could improve” if Trump’s Republican Party loses control of one or both chambers of Congress, potentially bringing greater scrutiny of the president’s agenda. In addition to halting the run of victories by the right and candidates backed by Trump, Lula interrupted another trend: a succession of defeats for incumbent governments, a phenomenon common over the past decade. That raises a broader question about whether the rightward shift is a lasting wave or part of a political pendulum. “Lula’s victory shows that the far right, particularly Bolsonaro’s movement, has a ceiling of support, because many voters consider it too radical,” Paarlberg said. He added that the result also suggests that backing from the White House and its battery of economic measures “are not decisive factors” in an election. In a Latin America increasingly defined by emerging leaders, Lula remains a statesman with international reach and one of the region’s key figures on the global stage. After another political feat, the record-breaking president has two months before beginning his fourth term to decide what course he will seek to chart for South America’s largest country over the next four years.

articles.title: Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case
articles.summary: The attack in eastern Dr Congo is the latest on health workers and responders to the deadly Ebola outbreak.
articles.body:
A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.

It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.

The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.

“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.

The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.

“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”

Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.

Data from the DRC’s Ministry of Health indicate that more than 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths, have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.

The government’s handling of the outbreak, combined with chronic corruption, has sown widespread distrust, with some even dismissing Ebola as a hoax.

Responders say scepticism about the disease among communities has complicated their efforts, including in remote areas and emerging hotspots already facing shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.

Last month, a DRC politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had called on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand-washing, on a radio show.

In May, at the start of the outbreak, angry residents set alight two tents at health centres in two separate attacks in just one week.

Responders say some residents have held captive or threatened team members in designated health zones.

The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central ⁠⁠and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

On Sunday, Uganda’s Minister of Health Chris Baryomunsi announced that all citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to the DRC will be quarantined for 21 days.

Uganda says it is ⁠Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July. But health experts remain on alert after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.

The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo , has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In an October 23 update, it urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.
