articles.title: ‘He can barely walk’: Russians tell how vulnerable men are being targeted and coerced into signing up
articles.summary: Since 2022, Russia has relied mostly on financial incentives to lure soldiers to fight. Evidence suggests that is now slowly giving way to coercion and deception.
articles.body: “They put him in the car and forced him to sign a contract…” “Now he’s listed as missing… I haven’t fully accepted that he is most likely already dead.” “It’s a paralyzing fear.” All of these are quotes from people who say they have personal experience of forced military recruitment in Russia. Their stories, told directly to CNN and backed up by human rights groups and a growing body of accounts from individuals and social media, paint a picture of a quiet shift underway in Russia’s war recruitment machine, now in its fifth year. We are obscuring their identities over their fear of reprisals. Since a mass mobilization drive in 2022, which sparked a panicked exodus across its borders, Russia has relied mostly on large financial incentives to lure soldiers to fight. Evidence suggests that is now slowly giving way to coercion and deception. Russia has repeatedly dismissed Ukrainian claims it is planning a new wave of mass mobilization, despite rising frontline casualties and falling recruitment numbers. And yet, as Russia escalates attacks, this “creeping mobilization” – as some are calling it – threatens to erode public acceptance of the war, just as the Kremlin needs it most. Vulnerable targets “I have (or rather I had) an uncle,” reads the message to CNN. “He is an old sick man, he has vascular problems and alcoholism, he can barely walk.” In July, the person said, their uncle, an employee at a state defense company in his late 50s, was approached outside his apartment block by several men in civilian clothes and taken away in a car. They didn’t know where he was taken, but said that day “they slipped him a document to sign, supposedly a ‘notification that they were there.’ It turned out to be a contract (to join the military).” The story, from a town in western Russia, fits an all-too-familiar pattern, said Artem Klyga, a Russian military lawyer based in Berlin, who advises Russians on their rights when it comes to military service. Since the start of the summer, he said, he has seen a surge in people reaching out to him about this kind of incident. “Now it’s a day-to-day practice,” he told CNN. Most cases he sees involve vulnerable men, often in debt or with health or alcohol problems. “They simply do not have a chance to say no, simply do not know their rights.” “Call to Conscience,” a coalition of lawyers helping conscripts and reservists in Russia with advice around conscientious objection, told CNN they had seen a surge in reports of forced recruitment in July and August, with tactics “getting harsher by the day.” In this case, after signing the document, the uncle returned home, his relative said, but a week later he disappeared. A few days after that he called to say he was at a training ground in Luhansk, in Russian-controlled eastern Ukraine. In late September came the news he was missing in action. “I have trouble falling asleep, sometimes I have nightmares that they catch me,” the relative told CNN. Another Russian who contacted CNN via a human-rights group said their brother was “detained” in mid-July “in a state of alcoholic intoxication, by unknown employees” – the relative’s assumption being that they worked for the local military recruitment office. In this case, CNN has seen the military contract the brother ended up signing, as well as a video of what appears to be his last goodbye to his tearful mother before he gets into a white van. The relative also shared the written response from the local military prosecutor’s office to the family’s petition for the man to be released. It concludes he appeared at the recruitment office “of his own free will, without any coercion,” adding that “the contrary has neither been proven nor documented.” Less than a month later came the news that he, too, was missing in action. “He had a very difficult life, problems with alcohol,” the relative told CNN. In June, Russia’s Penza region, about 375 miles south of Moscow, emerged as a particular hotspot for forced recruitment, according to social media accounts and human rights groups. Videos and accounts surfaced online of individuals being forcefully recruited off the streets. In one video from June which CNN has geolocated to a military recruitment center in Penza, women crowd around a bus demanding the men inside be released. One woman points inside the bus: “What do you think, did they sign voluntarily or not?” she shouts at the camera. One of the men inside the bus seems to shake his head. “They forced you, they beat you,” shouts another woman. The Russian Ministry of Defense dismissed the reports of forced mobilization in Penza as fake. Reports of violence in cases of forced recruitment are common, as is a disregard for medical exemptions. “The contract was signed under physical and moral pressure,” wrote one relative, who told CNN their uncle was taken in August. At the time he had a broken rib, they said. ‘Bring a friend’ bonuses Another common feature of many of these stories: the individuals taking men on the street are not clearly identified, and are often in civilian clothes. This has raised concerns that they could be ordinary people trying to cash in on another type of military bonus – paid to anyone helping recruit new soldiers. One relative described them as “bounty hunters.” CNN has not been able to verify this in specific cases, but regional authorities are making no attempt to hide the fact these payments exist. “We will encourage those who provide assistance in attracting citizens to sign contracts,” announced Pavel Malkov, the governor of Russia’s Ryazan region, last August in a session of the regional parliament. “We will provide a financial payment for each contract soldier. The bonus sum will vary from 50,000 to 300,000 rubles ($590 to $3,500), this is after tax.” CNN has found evidence of these official payments in multiple regions, as well as dozens of job ads offering recruiters large sums for each candidate who signs a military contract, with payouts varying by region. “It’s literally a ‘bring a friend’ kind of promotion, where you just find someone – anyone, in any state; in other words, it could be a drunk, a homeless person, or just about anyone – you drag them to the enlistment office, force them to sign a contract, and get your money,” said the founders of New Alternative Route, an anti-war organization set up this spring. Founded by Russian IT professionals in self-exile, it works to collate information on forced mobilization practices and advise people trying to leave Russia. Its representatives also spoke anonymously to CNN, out of fear for their families still in Russia. ‘I panicked a bit’ Russia has for years tried to differentiate itself from Ukraine, where conscription is mandatory from the age of 25 to 60 for men who are fit, and where reports have surfaced of incidents of press-ganging: violent or coercive mobilization. “We see every day on the television and on the internet how in Ukraine they catch people, like homeless dogs, and drag them forcefully to the front, said Russian President Vladimir Putin in early September. “Here people go voluntarily, as you know, and sign contracts.” With Russia’s military recruitment managed at a regional level via quotas, this rise in coercive tactics is unlikely to be directed by the Kremlin, said Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia Division at the German Institute for International and Security affairs, and yet it may be seen as a convenient solution to Russia’s manpower problem. “The system where essentially the recruiters are doing the dirty work… is at least tolerated,” by those at the top, he told CNN. “It could be, in the eyes of the authorities, part of the solution.” Russia’s Ministry of Defense has not responded to CNN’s request for comment. And yet, in the eyes of some Russians, it’s a tipping point. Rights groups told CNN that inquiries about how to emigrate are rising. Igor, a 21-year-old from central Russia for whom CNN is using a pseudonym over fears for his family’s safety, left the country three months ago, after years of planning to escape what he calls the “totalitarian madness.” In the year before he left, he said he had been pressured twice to sign military contracts – once by his university, and then on a visit to his local military recruitment office to update his medical exemption. “I panicked a bit,” he told CNN. “I worried that someone might sign on my behalf. I wouldn’t have been able to do anything about it.” The fear of a new wave of mass mobilization also brought urgent practical concerns. “I was afraid they’d close the border and I’d never be able to leave,” he told CNN. “I don’t think we’re going to see a scenario where we suddenly recruit 300,000 people tomorrow,” the founders of the New Alternative Route told CNN. Instead, they predict “a quiet, creeping mobilization driven by coercive measures. In other words, what happened in Penza… it’s all preparation.”

articles.title: Israel’s election: Five key things to know
articles.summary: Vote comes as Israel is embroiled in multiple wars, faces international criticism and grapples with domestic divisions.
articles.body:
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday for legislative elections.

The vote, the first since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, is being called one of the most important in its history .

It will determine the direction of Israel’s government as the country remains embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening polarisation at home.

Here are five things to know about the upcoming election:

Which are the main parties and what do opinion polls suggest?

Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, whose term lasts four years.

There are two main blocs vying to lead the next government.

The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and joined by several far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These include United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas – both conservative religious parties – and Otzma Yehudi and Religious Zionism-Zehut, led respectively by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

The main opposition coalition comprises four Jewish-led opposition movements – the Yashar party, led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the Democrats, led by former deputy military chief of staff Yair Golan, the Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by former Finance Minister Avigdor Lieberman and the Together alliance, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and joined by Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid.

The latest opinion polls published before a ban on new surveys took effect on Friday showed that neither bloc was on course to secure a parliamentary majority of 61 seats.

A poll by public broadcaster KAN projected that the opposition alliance would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc, with the remaining seats going to unaffiliated parties, including the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, and the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al parties.

However, both the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs have effectively ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties for now.

The fractured landscape means Israeli parties could be in for tough post-election negotiations to cobble together a governing majority. If those efforts fail, Israel could end up with a minority government reliant on support from parties outside the governing coalition – or potentially head to another round of elections.

Israelis are grappling with a series of domestic and international crises this election cycle.

On the domestic front, there is growing demand for accountability for reported security failures, including those leading up to the October 2023 attacks, anger over the growing ultra-Orthodox community’s military exemption and concern over Netanyahu’s repeated efforts to push judicial reforms that critics say undermine Israel’s liberal democratic order.

“The secular and liberal opposition factions in Israel feel this election is the last chance to save Israeli democracy and restore the institutions that have eroded over Netanyahu’s successive terms,” Mairav Zonszein, an Israeli-American commentator who is a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

A war-weary public is also weighing how Israel should proceed with its multiple military conflicts, with many voters seeking security and economic stability while remaining resistant to perceived concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.

It is Israel’s first election since the October 2023 attacks and comes amid a surge in far-right attitudes and growing divisions over the direction of the country.

“Strains of Israeli society had always been given to violence and right-wing rhetoric, but the trends that had always been present had accelerated under the current government,” prominent Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani told Al Jazeera.

The election also comes as Israel’s international standing has deteriorated, with a host of Israel’s allies sanctioning its illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, and many other nations denouncing the country’s continued attacks in Gaza and Lebanon.

When Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, dozens of envoys from around the world walked out , some jeering and booing.

The outcome of the upcoming vote could determine whether Israel’s next government maintains its approach to the international community or seeks to repair ties.

What does it mean for Netanyahu’s political future?

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for more than 15 of the last 17 years, and a total of 19, faces growing scrutiny at home and abroad over alleged security failures leading up to the October 7 attack, as well as corruption charges he has been battling since 2019.

An electoral defeat would also leave Netanyahu more exposed to his ongoing corruption trial, which could ultimately result in a prison sentence if he is convicted.

A new government could also affect the prospects of a potential commission of inquiry into the October 2023 attacks and Netanyahu’s political standing as he faces an arrest warrant for war crimes issued by the International Criminal Court.

What about Palestinian citizens of Israel?

About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million.

Meanwhile, roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no say in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.

Recent polling suggested that the turnout among the Palestinian citizens of Israel could reach 60 percent, with the majority of the votes expected to go the Arab lists, which are the principal representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel. If turnout reaches 65 percent, these parties could potentially win as many as 15 seats in the Knesset. Campaigners are aiming for 70 percent turnout, which would be the highest in decades and raise the threshold, keeping smaller parties out of parliament.

Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the Joint List and Ra’am from the election.

Israel’s top court quickly reversed that decision, enabling the Arab parties to stay in the race. However, the court did force Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the race over an article in which he described the October 7 attacks as “an important historical event”.

The role of Arab parties is going to be significant. Both major coalitions have ruled out joining forces with them for now, but without them, neither coalition might be able to form a majority.

Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray his opponents as potential partners of the Arab parties, claiming that an opposition-led government will seek their support and that only his Likud party can prevent this.

Joseph Mansour, a former aide to Israeli Knesset member Ayman Odeh, said politically alienating Arab parties is part of Netanyahu’s political strategy, which could allow him to remain in office as a caretaker prime minister if neither coalition forms a majority.

“If Palestinian-led party support becomes politically toxic and the opposition falls short of 61 seats, the deadlock itself becomes the latest win for Netanyahu,” wrote Mansour for the Arab Center Washington DC.

articles.title: Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
articles.summary: Serbia’s longtime leader concedes defeat to a student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections.
articles.body:
Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years.

After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years.

“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List.

The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.

The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights.

During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.

Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia.

A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years.

Born in Belgrade in 1970, the nearly 2-metre-tall (6.5ft-tall) Vucic graduated from the University of Belgrade’s faculty of law. He entered politics in 1993, joining the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party led by Vojislav Seselj.

His political record during the 1990s was marked by nationalist rhetoric. One of his most remembered statements came in Serbia’s parliament in July 1995, nine days after the Srebrenica genocide : “Kill one Serb, and we will kill 100 Muslims.” Vucic made the comments during a debate on possible NATO strikes against positions held by the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Vucic’s political mentor at the time, Seselj, was sentenced in 2018 to 10 years in prison by the Appeals Chamber of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals for persecution, deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serbs during the wars in the Balkans in the 1990s.

Aleksandar Seselj, the son of Vojislav Seselj, was on Vucic’s electoral list in Sunday’s elections.

After a split within the Serbian Radical Party, Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic founded the SNS in 2008. The new party sought to move closer to mainstream European politics.

Safeta Bisevac, a Serbian journalist who has long followed Vucic’s political career, believes he was initially less popular than Nikolic, who appeared closer to common citizens.

“Vucic lagged far behind in popularity at the time and was essentially the organiser of the newly formed party,” Bisevac told Al Jazeera.

In 2012, the SNS came to power promising to fight corruption, organised crime and abuses committed under previous governments.

One of the most prominent cases was the December 2012 arrest of businessman Miroslav Miskovic and his son Marko on suspicion of financial irregularities and tax evasion. After years of legal proceedings, both were acquitted and the state paid them compensation.

Bisevac said the results of the fight against corruption remained modest while the authorities expanded their control over institutions, the media and political life.

Vucic served as first deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2014 before ascending to the post of prime minister in 2014. Three years later, he became president of Serbia and won re-election in 2022. His term was due to run until 2027.

Under pressure from the student-led protests, he resigned in September and called early elections. Although the Serbian presidency is constitutionally limited, Vucic has retained a dominant influence over his party and state policy.

“He made many promises and fulfilled few of them, but in the meantime, he established almost complete control over the state apparatus,” Bisevac said.

Economic growth and the debate over living standards

The Serbian economy has expanded significantly since Vucic took Serbia’s political centre stage in 2012. Unemployment dropped from 26 percent to 8 to 9 percent while nominal gross domestic product nearly tripled, reaching about 90 billion euros ($101bn), according to official data cited by the Reuters news agency.

Annual foreign direct investment inflows rose from about 800 million euros ($896m) in 2012 to a record 5.2 billion euros ($5.8bn) in 2024.

A network of modern motorways has also been built.

However, rising wages have not necessarily translated into a proportional improvement in living standards. The rising cost of living and public debt remain important elements of the debate over the government’s economic record.

Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said “the students simply gave a voice to the justified anger of citizens.”

Speaking to Al Jazeera about Vucic’s policies, Radosavljevic said the past decade was characterised by “systematic pressure and the destruction of social institutions”.

“State intelligence services have spent less time on their actual duties and more time monitoring political opponents while critical thinking has been pushed out of the public media,” Radosavljevic said.

articles.title: What are the unanswered questions around the River Tyne nurdle spill?
articles.summary: The spill of 18 tonnes of plastic pellets happened in July but there is still a lot we do not know.
articles.body:
On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of about one billion tiny balls, spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.

It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.

In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.

But several questions remain. So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?

What is a nurdle and why do they matter?

Port of Tyne criticised over nurdle spill response

Nurdles clean-up volunteers meet Port of Tyne boss

A wind turbine installation vessel called the Wind Orca collided with a container ship berthed at the Port of Tyne.

A gantry crane on the quayside collapsed and ended up lying across the ship.

Two containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles. These are pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.

About 18 tonnes of these pellets spilled into the water because of the crash.

Northumbria Police said it was investigating the collision and so far, no-one has been arrested. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch is also investigating.

The Port of Tyne previously said it, along with others, had asked the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to consider enforcing safer transportation methods for nurdles , something environmental groups have long called for.

How much of the nurdles can actually be recovered?

By the end of September about 28% of the nurdles had been recovered, according to scientists.

But the Port of Tyne, the Environment Agency and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) said the numbers of nurdles washing up ashore had already "reduced significantly" by then and numbers were continuing to fall.

They said they believed the full recovery of the 18 tonnes was not achievable. When asked what percentage recovery rate would be considered a success, the bodies said they would measure success via various metrics including shoreline surveys.

The pellets from the spill have been found along the English coast from Northumberland to North Yorkshire.

On Friday the Danish Environment Protection Agency confirmed pellets found on the country's western coast had also likely originated from the Tyne spill.

Dr Matthew Perks at Newcastle University and his colleagues are monitoring the movement of the nurdles and examining how the pellets may deteriorate in water.

The team's modelling so far suggests about one in eight of the billion nurdles remain in the Tyne estuary and high river flows could flush these microplastics downstream in the autumn.

Perks said this was a crucial opportunity to collect the pellets.

Nevertheless he said it was unclear how far some of the nurdles could really travel.

"As time goes by, it becomes more difficult to pinpoint the areas where these nodules are likely to be," he said.

It is also unclear when the nurdles will start breaking down into nanoplastics. "That will change the way they behave," he said.

Professor Bhavani Narayanaswamy at the Scottish Association for Marine Science said it could be months or years before we understood the full impact of the spill.

She said the nurdles could affect wildlife in various ways, including getting stuck in animal digestive tracts and adsorbing chemicals which then may be toxic to wildlife when ingested.

Prof Narayanaswamy said there was little research on the long-term impact of plastic pollution on animals compared with its immediate effects.

Dan Turner, who coordinates the North East England Beached Bird Survey, said the group had collected several dead birds along the coast which they would be testing for nurdles next month.

"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs," he previously told the BBC .

Recovery is largely being paid for by insurers representing BG Orange, which was carrying the pellets, as well as local councils and the Port of Tyne.

Thousands of volunteers have also been involved in the clean-up.

Councils have been told to record their costs so they can seek compensation from the insurers of those ultimately found responsible.

The multi-agency group, consisting of the North East MSA, Port of Tyne and the EA, said the nurdle recovery programme was continuing but it had increasingly moved away from "large-scale clean-up activity" towards "targeted recovery and monitoring".

Environmental charity Fidra said it was unclear how long the clean-up would need to continue, considering the fact that nurdles could stay in water for years.

It said a long-term plan was required to tackle the pollution and the plans should be "adequately resourced" with responsibility clearly defined.

Is it still worth going to beach cleans?

Volunteer Lou Shackleton said there was still a core group of individuals who gave up their spare time to monitor and recover nurdles on local beach.

She said the group needed all the help they could get.

"If you're happy to wrap up against the rain and the wind... come and join us," she said.

Follow BBC North East on X , Facebook , Nextdoor and Instagram and listen on BBC Sounds .

Autumn river levels could move nurdles downstream

Only 28% of nurdles 'recovered', researchers say

Offenders help clear nurdles after major spill

articles.title: Fed-up Shrewsbury driver builds AI litter tracker
articles.summary: Robin Bennett says he created the app after getting frustrated by the amount of rubbish beside roads
articles.body:
A software developer became so frustrated by the amount of rubbish he saw dumped along roadsides that he built an AI-powered "litter dashcam" to expose the scale of the problem.

Robin Bennett, from Shrewsbury, developed the Roadside Litter app after noticing what he believed was a growing amount of litter while driving around the county.

The technology has already logged more than 3,000 litter reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 across the UK.

He is now sharing the data with anti-litter campaign group Clean Up Britain in the hope it will encourage action, while Shropshire Council said it was exploring ways to improve litter management on some of the county's busiest roads.

Bennett, who runs a software company in Telford, said he found the amount of rubbish on local roads "really depressing" and wanted to understand whether the issue was unique to Shropshire or part of a wider national problem.

After approaching Clean Up Britain to ask how he could help, he went on to develop what he describes as a "litter dashcam" that records rubbish spotted from a vehicle.

"My software company's created an app, which essentially is a litter dashcam," he said.

"The app records the litter that it sees."

Mounted on a vehicle dashboard, the app automatically takes a photograph every 10 seconds, identifying visible litter and grading it against a national standard before uploading the information.

Bennett said: "I've got a phone holder stuck to the dashboard, I've put my phone in securely.

"I start it and that's it, you don't have to touch the screen, and the screen will go black in a minute so it's not distracting in any way.

"Every 10 seconds it takes a photo, it looks at the litter it can see by the side of the road and it grades it according to a national standard."

The app had recorded more than 3,000 reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 nationwide, Bennett said.

He added litter was particularly common near convenience stores, fast-food outlets and motorway service stations.

"People pick up a bag of fast food and just throw the bag out the window," he added.

Bennett said he hoped the data collected by the app would help build a clearer picture of the problem and encourage authorities to do more to tackle roadside litter.

A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said the authority recognised the importance of maintaining a clean and attractive highway network and was engaging with National Highways to explore opportunities to improve litter management on the A5 and A49.

articles.title: In 2020, a California homeowner sought permission to build a second living unit on his property; he says city delays lasted over three years and cost him more than $1 million, and an appeals court has revived his lawsuit
articles.summary: Adding a second home on an existing residential property is often presented as one of California’s simplest answers to its housing shortage.
articles.body: Adding a second home on an existing residential property is often presented as one of California’s simplest answers to its housing shortage. But for one homeowner in Palos Verdes Estates, the effort to build an accessory dwelling unit became a years-long permitting battle. A recent appellate ruling has now reopened his lawsuit, finding that California’s rules were designed to protect homeowners from precisely the kind of delays he says he experienced.A permit request that stretched for yearsAccording to the Judicial Branch of California, Shi first applied in 2020 for permission to construct an accessory dwelling unit, or ADU, on his property in the City of Palos Verdes Estates. He planned to complete the additional dwelling alongside construction of his family home.California law requires qualifying ADU applications to be considered through a ministerial process, without discretionary review or a hearing. The Judicial Branch of California notes that the applicable rules also require a permitting agency to approve or deny a completed application within 60 days when an existing dwelling is already on the property.Shi alleged that the city did not follow that process. Instead, he said, his application was subjected to additional planning requirements, including a conditional use permit, discretionary review and approval from the Palos Verdes Homes Association Art Jury.The city ultimately approved the ADU in 2023, more than three years after Shi initially applied, according to the Judicial Branch of California.More than $1 million in alleged lossesThe prolonged approval process had financial consequences, Shi alleged. The Judicial Branch of California reports that his claimed losses included the loss of use of his property, higher construction expenses, interest costs, professional design fees and a reduction in property value. Shi estimated that his total damages exceeded $1 million.He subsequently filed a lawsuit against the city under California’s Government Claims Act, arguing that the state’s ADU laws imposed a mandatory duty on local governments and that the city’s failure to comply with that duty caused his losses.A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge initially sided with the city. The trial court concluded that the ADU laws were primarily intended to address California’s housing shortage by making it easier to create additional homes, rather than protecting individual homeowners from financial losses caused by permitting delays.Appeals court revives the caseThe California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division Four, reached a different conclusion. In its October 23, 2026 published opinion, the court reversed the lower court’s judgment, according to the Judicial Branch of California.The appellate court determined that homeowners applying for ADU permits are direct beneficiaries of the state’s requirement for timely, ministerial approval. The court reasoned that preventing unnecessary delays is central to the purpose of the permitting rules, rather than merely an incidental benefit.The ruling also distinguished between the purpose of increasing California’s housing supply and the specific duty imposed on local governments. While ADUs serve the broader goal of addressing the housing crisis, the court found that the legislation also directly benefits homeowners seeking to construct them.What happens nextThe appeals court did not determine that Shi has already proved his damages or that the city is ultimately liable. Instead, it found that he had adequately alleged a cause of action and that his lawsuit should not have been dismissed at the earlier stage.The judgment in favour of the city was therefore reversed, with the Judicial Branch of California reporting that Shi is entitled to recover his costs on appeal.The decision could have wider significance for California homeowners seeking to add ADUs, particularly where local permitting processes appear to go beyond the streamlined framework established by state law. It also underscores the growing legal importance of the state’s efforts to make accessory housing easier and faster to build.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.
articles.body:
In the Chinese capital a major political gathering is underway, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.

The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.

The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.

The normally annual Plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.

They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.

There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.

The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.

Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.

The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.

Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.

This years plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.

Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past Plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.

This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.

Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.

"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".

The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.

The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.

This Plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.
